newsitem.title: USA: Prosecutor says lacks evidence on Kevorkian charges.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutor says lacks evidence on Kevorkian charges.

text.p: Jack Kevorkian will not be charged with assisting in the apparent suicides of two women last week unless police find evidence of his involvement, a prosecutor said on Tuesday.

Oakland County Prosecutor David Gorcyca said in a statement that witnesses and family members refused to cooperate with police investigations of the deaths of Elaine Day, 79, of Newhall, California, and Lisa Lansing, 42, of Floram, New Jersey.

Day's body was left in Kevorkian's battered Volkswagen van at the Oakland County morgue early on the morning of Feb. 3, less than two hours after Lansing's body was brought to a Pontiac hospital by a New Jersey friend.
Both Day and Lansing died from lethal injections. The Oakland County medical examiner has ruled Day's death a homicide but has not determined the manner of Lansing's death.
Kevorkian, who has attended at least 45 suicides since 1990 and has regularly dropped off bodies in his van and at hospital emergency rooms, has not admitted to any involvment in the deaths.
Gorcyca said not enough was known of the facts and circumstances of both deaths to issue arrest warrants.
"Dr. Kevorkian doesn't talk to the police," said Michael Schwartz, one of his attorneys. "They have shown nothing but poor behaviour towards him for years."
Schwartz said he was unaware of any involvement by Kevorkian and lauded Gorcyca for showing restraint.
But last week, Kevorkian's lead attorney, Geoffrey Fieger, told the Detroit News: "You have to have been born under a rock yesterday not to know who was involved in these cases."
Schwartz dismissed Fieger's statement as mere "banter" with a reporter and said it does not constitute an admission of Kevorkian's involvement.

However, the statement was enough to prompt Ionia County Prosecutor Raymond Voet to ask a judge to revoke Kevorkian's bond on separate charges, which would prohibit him from being present at additional suicides. A hearing on the request was planned for next week.
Kevorkian faces assisted suicide charges in the rural western Michigan county in the August 1996 death of Loretta Peabody, 54, a case expected to go to trial this spring.

Peabody's death was initially thought to be from natural causes related to multiple sclerosis, but a police raid on a Bloomfield Township, Mich., hotel room where Kevorkian was meeting with another patient turned up a videotape showing Peabody consulting with the suicide activist.
In a blow to the Ionia case against Kevorkian, authorities disclosed on Tuesday that DNA tests revealed that blood found on an armrest seized in the raid was not Peabody's.
